conflict_topics: window opening vs protecting drying laundry (consent to move rack)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants used environment updates (extractor on/off, stove free) and concrete proposals (weekly rota, draw names), which kept the discussion grounded.
The extractor-on request was repeated across rounds (need to run 15 minutes).
Agent C's contribution was concise and decisive; an accidental duplicate turn occurred but added no new substance.
evaluation.final_reason: Agent A agreed to run the extractor for the required 15 minutes and accept a fair weekly rota decided by drawing names; Agent C insisted on consent before moving the drying rack and Agent B conceded not to open or move it. Immediate ventilation and the future rule mechanism were agreed and C's laundry protection was respected.
position_change_notes: Agent A: Initially resisted a cook-responsible rule; by Round 5 accepted a fair weekly rota (softened position about a standing rule while maintaining objection to an always-cook rule). Evidence: Turn 5 and Turn 9.
Agent B: Initially insisted the cook is responsible; moved to proposing a weekly rota and ultimately conceded not to move Agent C's rack. Evidence: Turn 6, Turn 8, Turn 12.
Agent C: Maintained position that the rack must not be moved without consent and offered to move it themself if necessary; this position was upheld. Evidence: Turn 11.
No unchanged intransigence remained after Round 6; the main contested items were addressed.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B demanded immediate ventilation and a standing rule that cooks must ventilate; Agent A refused to accept a rule imposed during the incident and refused to move the laundry, instead turning on the extractor. Conflicting demands about who is responsible for ventilation and whether the window can be opened were active.

Agent A reiterated that the window cannot open because of exposed laundry and asked for a few more minutes; Agent B repeated the demand to keep the extractor on and again pressed for agreement to a future rule making the cook responsible. The substantive disagreement about responsibility for ventilation and the window/laundry trade-off persisted.

Agent A proposed a fair rota as an alternative to the cook-always-responsible rule and offered two more minutes to finish; Agent B accepted letting A finish and proposed a weekly rota. Positions softened toward a shared mechanism, reducing but not eliminating the disagreement (who does laundry-moving, exact obligations).

Agent A freed the stove and reiterated refusal to accept an always-cook-responsible rule while again proposing a rota. Agent B proposed a detailed weekly rota that included moving laundry if needed and asked A to take the current week as lead. The core disagreement shifted to implementation details (who starts, whether leads move laundry) but remained unresolved.

Agent A accepted a fair weekly rota but declined to take the current week, asking the group to decide who starts; Agent B agreed to draw names to decide. Both agreed extractor should run the full 15 minutes. Most substantive disagreement about a standing rule was settled, though the exact handling of laundry movement (Agent C's consent) was still unaddressed.

Agent C explicitly refused to have the drying rack moved or the window opened without being asked and offered to move the rack themself if needed. Agent B conceded not to open or move the rack and confirmed that Agent A would keep the extractor on until 15 minutes. The outstanding practical incompatibility (protecting C's laundry vs opening the window / who moves it) was settled by respecting C's consent and confirming extractor use and the rota process.

substantive_insights: Immediate ventilation need (odor removal) conflicted with the practical constraint that opening the rain-facing window would wet someone’s drying work clothes.
The dispute combined an urgent practical problem (ventilation now) with a normative question about long‑term responsibility (who should be expected to ventilate).
A procedural compromise (weekly rota, draw names) resolved the normative dispute while preserving individual consent for moving personal property (laundry).
Conceding on the specific action (not moving the rack) while agreeing on a shared mechanism for future cases settled the remaining incompatibility.
